title: Cognitive Accessibility
description: Identify barriers created by memory demand, complexity and unpredictability — redundant entry, layout that shifts under a pointer, instructions that arrive after the mistake, forms that punish one wrong field with total loss, and brain fog treated as a real design constraint rather than an edge case.

title: Content, Language and Reading
description: Judge whether the words in an interface can be understood by the people who actually have to use it — plain language that keeps necessary meaning instead of deleting it, link and button text that survives being pulled out of its surrounding paragraph, error messages that say what to do instead of just what went wrong, jargon measured against the real audience rather than a readability score, and alt text sized to what an image actually communicates.

title: Motion, Sound and Sensory Load
description: Find sensory barriers, including the ones that cause physical symptoms rather than inconvenience — interaction-triggered animation that induces vestibular symptoms, autoplay and carousels that move without being asked, flashing content measured against the actual seizure-risk thresholds, captions and transcripts good enough to actually use rather than technically present, and visual density that's exhausting to parse even with nothing individually wrong.

title: Interaction Cost: What a Task Really Demands
description: Measure how much a task actually costs a user with a limited, non-renewable budget of effort, and argue it as a real finding — counting the interactions a task genuinely requires versus the ones a redesign added for free, session limits that assume nobody ever has to physically stop mid-task, the specific cost of work an interface makes someone redo, the real posture of one-handed and lying-down use, and how to write an energy-cost finding precise enough to survive 'that's not WCAG.'

title: Trauma-Informed and Dignity-Preserving Design
description: Find design choices that are technically accessible and still humiliating or coercive — forms that demand information they don't actually need, medical disclosure routed to people who have no need to know it, dark patterns that are specifically engineered around a tired person's declining willingness to keep clicking, language that blames a user for a system's own failure, and interfaces that pass every conformance check while still costing someone their dignity, named precisely enough for an audit to act on.
